description: Team Stranded is six students from Dr. D.Y. Patil Institute of Technology, Pune. We built Lunar Statio, a south-pole mission planner that shows when a landing site has sunlight for power and Earth in view for communication, using NASA LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides, with every number checked against NASA references.
summary:
Lunar Statio is a browser-based mission planner for the Moon's south pole. For any spot between 85° and 90° S and any hour, it shows whether the Sun (power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth line of sight) are above the site's real terrain horizon, and how that changes over a lunar day, a month and a full year.

Near the pole the Sun skims within about 1.6° of the horizon, so a ridge kilometres away can cause days of darkness, and a short launch slip can turn a good site dark. The challenge asks for rapid comparison of sites and dates after a slip, and that is our core loop. Planners pick a site, set mission needs, and see every day marked viable, marginal or not viable. They can simulate slips, rank 5,487 candidate spots for a fixed date, check the whole landing ellipse, and compare scenarios side by side.

All results come from NASA LOLA terrain and JPL DE421 ephemerides, and the app runs with no backend. Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to within 0.000033°, and long-term sunlight matches NASA's LOLA illumination maps (r = 0.991). Landers like those in Artemis and commercial missions need answers that are fast and can be checked, and this tool gives them in seconds.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Statio is a mission-planning tool for the Moon's south pole that runs in the browser. For any spot between 85° and 90° S and any hour, it shows whether the Sun (for power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth line of sight) are above that site's real terrain horizon. It also shows how this changes over a lunar day, a lunar month and a full year of seasons.

It answers the questions a planner faces after a launch slip:

- Is this site sunlit and in view of Earth right now, and for how long?

- The launch slipped 14 days. Is the landing still viable, and when does the next window open?

- The date is fixed. Which spots nearby still meet our power and comms needs?

HOW IT WORKS

An offline Python pipeline computes Sun and Earth positions from the JPL DE421 ephemeris in the Moon's own reference frame (libration included). It traces a 360° terrain horizon for each site from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data (240 m near the pole), with lunar curvature included. It then works out how much of the Sun's and Earth's discs are visible for each of the 8,760 hours in a year. The browser runs a line-by-line port of the same maths in a Web Worker, so clicking anywhere on the south-pole map computes a new site's horizon and a full year of visibility. There is no server.

Main screens: a horizon dial (the terrain silhouette with Sun and Earth moving around it), a landing-date planner (every day marked viable / marginal / not viable, slip buttons, a "slip budget"), a site finder (ranks 5,487 candidate spots for your exact mission window), a landing-ellipse check, a south-pole map with NASA sunlight and Earth-visibility layers, 3D terrain with GPU-computed shadows, a scenario comparison with CSV/JSON export, and a solar recharge planner for rovers.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Near the pole the Sun stays within about 1.6° of the horizon, so a ridge kilometres away can bring days of darkness, and a slip of a few days can turn a good site dark. The data to answer this already exists, but it is spread across specialist tools. Lunar Statio puts the re-planning loop in one place and answers it in seconds. It is for Artemis and commercial lander teams, students, and the public.

ACCURACY

Every number is checked against an independent NASA reference: Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to within 0.000033°. Long-term sunlight matches NASA's LOLA illumination maps with r = 0.991, and Earth visibility with r = 0.995. The browser engine matches the Python pipeline to 3.49 × 10⁻⁷°. An in-app Validation page shows each check and how to rerun it. Mission replays of Chandrayaan-3 and IM-1 Odysseus put our model next to what ISRO and NASA reported.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (NumPy, Skyfield), TypeScript, React 19, Vite, three.js, CesiumJS, WebGL 2 shaders (GLSL), Web Workers, Canvas 2D and SVG. Hosted on Vercel, version-controlled on GitHub. Data: NASA LRO LOLA, JPL DE421 and NAIF kernels, JPL Horizons, NASA Goddard PGDA illumination maps, NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit, NASA Moon Trek. No special hardware: it runs on any laptop with a WebGL 2 browser.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- The horizon dial shows Sun and Earth moving like clock hands around the real terrain silhouette.

- 3D shadows are ray-marched on the GPU, because standard shadow maps are wrong when the Sun is 1–2° above the horizon.

- The "slip budget" tells a team how many days they can slip before a site stops being viable.

- The name comes from IAU naming practice: "Statio" is used for landing sites (Statio Tranquillitatis, Statio Shiv Shakti).

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Getting the science right came before features. No machine learning is used: every output is deterministic physics on public NASA/JPL data, so it can be reproduced and checked. Simplified models are labelled as simplified and visual scales as not to scale. Earth in view means geometric line of sight, not a guaranteed radio link. Limits are stated in the app: 240 m terrain, a 2 m mast, hourly time steps. The meaning colours (amber for Sun, blue for Earth, green for both) are safe for colour-blind users, controls work from the keyboard, and reduced-motion settings are respected.
